the bag still holds only what src held at construction time

options.misconception: believes any list assignment performs a defensive copy

questions.learningObjective: predict which overload a null literal selects

options.text: it calls Value(String), because String is the more specific parameter type
it reports an ambiguous reference and refuses to compile the line
options.misconception: believes two applicable reference overloads are always ambiguous

options.text: it calls Value(Object), because null matches any reference type equally
options.misconception: believes a supertype parameter wins when the argument is null

options.text: it reports an error, because null is not a valid constructor argument
options.misconception: believes a null literal cannot be passed to a constructor

questions.explanation: A null literal converts to both String and Object in the first resolution phase, and String is a subtype of Object, so the more specific signature wins and Value(String) is called. options.text: the class is missing a no-argument version, which the compiler substitutes for null
options.misconception: believes an absent constructor silently accepts a null argument

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: order static setup against per-object setup
questions.stem: A class declares, in source order, a static field, a static initializer block, an instance field with an initializer, an instance initializer block, and a constructor body. Which statement about when they run is true?

options.text: the static field then the static block run once at class setup, and each object then runs its field initializer, its instance block, and its constructor body in that order
each constructor body runs first, and the field initializers and blocks catch up afterwards
options.misconception: believes a constructor body precedes the field initializers

options.text: the static block runs once for every new object just before that object's constructor
options.misconception: believes static blocks are repeated per instance

options.text: the instance field initializers run once for the whole class, and the static items repeat per object
options.misconception: believes the two levels of initialization are swapped

questions.explanation: Class setup happens once, on the first active use of the class, and runs static field initializers and static blocks in declaration order. Only after that does each new object run its own field initializers, then its instance initializer blocks, then its constructor body, which is why the constructor cannot run before the fields exist and why static state is never rebuilt per object.
questions.hint: Split the members into class level and object level first.

options.misconception: believes blocks are hoisted ahead of field initializers

options.text: 1, because a static field initializer only runs at the first use of a field
options.misconception: believes a static field initializer waits for a field read

options.misconception: believes the method's increment cancels the earlier value

questions.stem: A designer wants creation to validate its input, hand back one shared instance for repeated equal values, and let a caller choose a subtype at the point of creation. Which capability belongs to a static factory method but not to a constructor?

options.text: it can return a cached instance, or an instance of some other type entirely
it can reject a bad argument by throwing an exception
options.misconception: believes only a factory can validate its input

options.text: it can assign every final field of the object it produces
options.misconception: believes a factory can set fields a constructor cannot

options.text: it can run before the produced object's fields have been assigned
options.misconception: believes a factory can observe a half-built object

the write is rejected, because final makes the contents of the array constant
options.misconception: believes final on a field freezes whatever it points at

options.text: the write is legal only when the method that performs it is static
options.misconception: believes final writes are restricted to static methods

options.text: the write is rejected, because a final array must be sized where it is declared
options.misconception: believes final arrays may not be written after construction

questions.learningObjective: explain the final-field guarantee for another thread
questions.stem: A class assigns its final fields inside the constructor and then hands the new object to another thread with no locking and no volatile. Why does marking those fields final matter?

options.text: correctly written final fields are frozen when construction ends, so the reader is guaranteed to see them
final fields are kept in a shared static area, so every read is always current
options.misconception: believes final fields live outside the object

options.text: the final keyword makes the object's methods run inside the reader's thread first
options.misconception: believes final reruns the constructor on the reading thread

options.text: without final the reader could still see the constructor's writes, so final is only a style choice
options.misconception: believes the visibility guarantee needs no keyword at all

questions.explanation: The freeze that follows a constructor in which final fields are assigned gives a reader that obtains the reference a guarantee that those writes are visible, without any synchronization on the reader's side. The guarantee covers exactly the fields declared final and assigned during construction, which is why non-final fields carry no such promise and must be published another way.
questions.hint: Think about what the reader can be certain of after obtaining the reference.

options.misconception: believes equals alone governs membership in a hashed set

options.misconception: believes a getClass test fails against the class that wrote it

questions.learningObjective: justify an invariant repaired inside a method
questions.stem: A class promises that its total always equals the sum of its parts. A private method assigns total from the parts, and a public method calls that private method. Why is the promise still trustworthy?

options.text: no outside code can observe the moment between the two assignments, because the fields are private
the compiler re-checks the promise after every private method returns
options.misconception: believes the compiler verifies field relationships

options.text: private methods only run after the constructor, so the state starts consistent
options.misconception: believes private methods are deferred until later

options.text: the promise covers only field values, so intermediate values do not count
options.misconception: believes an invariant says nothing about intermediate states

questions.learningObjective: diagnose a silent set lookup failure
questions.practice: error analysis on a hash collection
questions.stem: A class overrides equals to compare its two fields and never overrides hashCode. A test adds one instance to a HashSet, adds an equal instance, and finds the set reports size 1 while contains with an equal instance reports false. Which claim explains both results?

options.text: identity hash codes put the two equal instances in different buckets, so the lookup misses
the set compares with equals first, so it wrongly rejected the second instance
options.misconception: believes equality is checked before the bucket is chosen

options.text: a hash code must be derived from the printed form, so the buckets collided instead
options.misconception: believes toString feeds the bucket choice

options.text: overriding equals makes the inherited hash code follow the fields automatically
options.misconception: believes the two overrides are linked by the compiler

questions.explanation: The inherited hash code comes from Object and is based on identity, so the two equal instances hash differently; the second add therefore creates a second entry, which is why the size grows, and the lookup lands in the wrong bucket and never calls equals. The two overrides are a package deal: overriding equals means also deriving hash code from the same fields.
questions.hint: Ask which value decides the bucket each add and each lookup inspects.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a map entry lost after a key field changed
questions.practice: error analysis on a mutable key
questions.stem: A customer class is used as a key in a HashMap, and its name is a mutable field that both equals and hashCode read. After the customer's name is edited, get with an equal new instance returns null. Why?

options.text: the stored key's hash code changed, so the lookup lands in a bucket the map never scans
the map compares keys only with equals, and the edited key now reports unequal
options.misconception: believes the map finds the entry and then reports unequal

options.text: a hash map drops any key whose fields change while the map is in use
options.misconception: believes the map watches keys and evicts changed ones

options.text: the edited key was stored twice, so the map holds two entries for one customer
options.misconception: believes editing a key inserts a second entry

questions.explanation: A hash collection picks a bucket from the hash code, and the stored key's hash code now differs from that of the equal lookup key, so the map never compares the two and returns null. Keys used in a HashMap or HashSet have to be immutable, which is one more reason a value object is usually the right thing to key on.
questions.hint: Ask which bucket each of the two keys now hashes into.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a read-only list that grew on its own
questions.practice: error analysis on a live view
questions.stem: A caller stores the read-only list returned by shelf.items() and keeps it for the length of a session. Later the shelf adds an item, and the caller's stored list now contains an entry the caller never added. Why?

options.text: the method returned a read-only view over the shelf's live list rather than a copy
the method returned a copy, and the shelf reached back and changed that copy
options.misconception: believes the shelf holds a reference to a list it handed out

options.text: the read-only list shares its storage with every other list built the same way
options.misconception: believes read-only lists are all views of one shared list

options.text: the shelf rebuilt its own field, so the old list was reused for the new items
options.misconception: believes reassigning a field recycles the caller's list

questions.explanation: Collections.unmodifiableList wraps the original list rather than copying it, so both names point at one set of entries and any addition the shelf makes is visible through the caller's stored reference; the wrapper blocks writes, not reads of later changes. If callers must see a frozen snapshot the method has to build a new list, and if they must see live contents the shelf has to accept that the view will grow.
questions.hint: Ask whether the returned object has storage of its own.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a swapped precondition exception type
questions.stem: A class has a constructor that throws IllegalArgumentException for a negative size and a submit method that throws IllegalStateException before the record is opened. A caller reports catching the wrong type for a bad size. Which contract puts the reporting right?

options.text: keep the size check as an argument precondition and the open check as a state precondition
throw IllegalStateException for both, since both describe the object's condition
options.misconception: believes a rejected parameter is a condition problem

options.text: throw IllegalArgumentException for both, since both are mistakes made by the caller
options.misconception: believes every refusal is an argument problem

options.text: return an error code from both instead of throwing, so no exception type applies
options.misconception: believes the distinction disappears if nothing is thrown

questions.explanation: A negative size is a bad parameter and belongs to the method's argument precondition, so IllegalArgumentException is the type a caller can catch to mean you passed me something impossible; calling submit too early is about the object's own condition and belongs to IllegalStateException. Collapsing the two into one type throws away the distinction that lets a caller react differently to a fixable input and a not-yet-ready object.
questions.hint: Ask whether the caller should fix a value or finish a process.
